readerTitle: The risk that keeps a restaurant owner up at night is rarely the biggest one
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 식당, 레스토랑용 예약 소프트웨어 회사) · 모든 점수는 설명용
insight: 가장 생생하게 떠오르는 위험보다, 확률과 충격을 곱한 값이 크고 대체할 수 없는 한 사람·한 설비에 걸린 위험을 먼저 다룬다.
misconception: 악성 리뷰나 도난처럼 눈에 띄고 무서운 위험이 가장 큰 위험이다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨: OPS-07-02 확률 × 영향, OPS-07-04 단일 장애 지점
모든 점수와 상황은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 3번 카드의 확률·영향 점수(1~5)는 설명용 가정이며 실제 업계 통계가 아닙니다. 계산 확인: 악성 리뷰 2×2=4, 도난 2×3=6, 냉장고 고장 3×4=12, 셰프 갑작스런 퇴사 3×5=15.
실제 사고 빈도나 손실 금액은 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다. 특정 국가의 보험·노동법 조언으로 읽히지 않도록 7번 카드에서 보험은 별도 레슨(OPS-07-03)으로만 언급했습니다.

cards.title: The risk that keeps a restaurant owner up at night is rarely the biggest one
body: Maya runs a 40-seat bistro. At 2 a.m. she worries about a one-star review going viral, or someone breaking in.
Her real exposure sits somewhere quieter: in the walk-in cooler humming in the back, and in the one person who knows every sauce by heart.

image.label: Restaurant owner at night with worry bubbles over a quiet kitchen
image.brief: 밤의 식당 주방. 주인이 계산대에 앉아 있고, 머리 위 말풍선에 별 하나짜리 리뷰와 깨진 창문. 뒤쪽 어둠 속에 대형 냉장고와 셰프 앞치마가 조용히 걸려 있음. 실제 리뷰 사이트 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You can fix one thing this month.
body: Maya has a small budget and one free afternoon for risk. Three options are on her list.

options.text: Write a social media plan for a viral bad review
options.feedback: It feels urgent because it's vivid. But using **probability times impact**, most bad reviews do limited, short-lived damage.

options.text: Add a temperature alarm and a repair contract for the walk-in cooler
options.feedback: A cooler failure is fairly likely over a few years, and it can spoil a week of stock and close the kitchen. Moderate probability times high impact puts it near the top.
A real risk, and worth handling. But the likely loss is cash and equipment, so its probability times impact scores lower than the cooler.

cards.title: The biggest risk wasn't on her list.
body: Maya scores each risk from 1 to 5 for how likely it is in a year and how badly it would hurt. Rough guesses are enough. Then she multiplies.

cards.title: Probability times impact
body: Our attention goes to risks that are dramatic or recent. **Probability times impact** corrects for that. A rare disaster and a common nuisance can score the same. A fairly common event that hurts a lot beats both.
The scores don't need to be precise. Their job is to rank, so the conversation moves from "what scares me" to "what would cost me most."

cards.title: Look for the one thing everything depends on.
body: Maya's top two risks share a pattern. Each is a **single point of failure**: one part with no backup, whose loss stops the whole kitchen.
list: One head chef who holds the recipes and the ordering
One cooler holding all the perishable stock
One produce supplier with one delivery van
One owner with the only bank login
cards.callout: Ask of each: if this vanished tomorrow, could we open tonight?
cards.softwareNote: In software the same pattern shows up as one server, one cloud region, or one engineer who holds the keys. The fix is the same: a documented backup.

cards.title: Only Daniel knows the sauces.
body: Head chef Daniel built the menu. The recipes live in his head, and he places every supplier order himself. If he left with two weeks' notice, the kitchen would struggle.

options.text: Give Daniel a raise so he stays
options.feedback: It lowers the probability he leaves, but not the impact if he does. The **single point of failure** is still there.

options.text: Have Daniel write down recipes and train the sous chef on ordering
options.feedback: This shrinks the impact of his leaving, sickness or holiday. It removes the **single point of failure** instead of guarding it.

options.text: Hire a second head chef as backup
options.feedback: It removes the dependency, but at a cost that may outweigh the risk. Redundancy should fit the **probability times impact**, not exceed it.

cards.title: You can't back up everything.
body: Every backup costs money or time. A second cooler, a second supplier, a cross-trained cook: each is worth it only if the risk it covers scores high enough.

And some risks score low because they're rare, like a kitchen fire, yet could end the business. Scoring alone won't handle those. They call for insurance or a plan to keep running, which other lessons in this unit cover.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your five-person company sells table-booking software to restaurants. Three worries are on the board.

options.text: A bigger rival might launch a cheaper product
options.feedback: Plausible, but slow-moving and hard to prevent this month. Its **probability times impact** is real but you can't fix it quickly.

options.text: Only one engineer can deploy fixes or restore the database
options.feedback: If she's sick during an outage, restaurants lose bookings on a Friday night. It's a **single point of failure** with high impact and an easy fix: documentation and shared access.

options.text: A security breach that makes the news
options.feedback: Vivid and serious, but basic security may already lower its probability. Don't let the headline crowd out the quieter, likelier failure.

cards.softwareNote: This is the same pattern as Daniel's sauces: knowledge held by one person.

cards.title: Rank risks by the math, then hunt for what has no backup.
body: **Concepts used:** probability times impact, to rank risks by cost rather than fear. Single points of failure, to find the one person or part that can stop everything.
**Try it today:** list your top five risks, score each 1–5 for likelihood and impact, and circle any that depend on one person or one machine.

image.brief: 손으로 쓴 위험 목록 메모지. 각 항목 옆에 점수(4, 6, 12, 15)가 적혀 있고, '셰프'와 '냉장고' 항목에 빨간 동그라미. 따뜻한 색감의 일러스트.
